claim: Every physical location has a corresponding spiritual city.
reading: Daniel 10 associates spiritual conflict with named kingdoms.
distinction: The passage does not state a universal one-to-one map of physical places and spiritual cities.

claim: Thrones are elders who guard God's secrets.
reading: Colossians 1:16 names thrones. Revelation 4 portrays elders on thrones worshipping God.
distinction: Connecting these into one universal job description is an interpretation, rather than a definition supplied in Colossians.

claim: Dominions are territorial governors or ambassadors.
reading: Colossians 1:16 includes dominions among creation subject to Christ.
distinction: The verse does not specify their territorial assignments or define them as ambassadors.

claim: Principalities are first-comers or warrior generals reclaiming territories.
reading: Ephesians 6 names hostile principalities. Daniel 10 describes conflict involving princes.
distinction: A detailed pioneer or general role is the proposed framework. These passages do not provide that definition.

claim: Demons possess people while principalities possess territories and wear spiritual garments.
reading: The New Testament records demonic affliction. Daniel 10 connects princes with kingdoms.
distinction: These accounts do not establish an exclusive people-versus-territories classification or a doctrine of territorial spiritual garments.

claim: Rulers of darkness write cultural laws requiring higher-rank watchmen to overcome them.
reading: Ephesians 6 names rulers of darkness and calls believers to armour and persevering prayer. Acts 19 shows worship, money and public pressure influencing a city.
distinction: The specified magistrate mechanism and rank requirement are not stated here. Prayer, holiness and practical resistance to corruption remain biblical responsibilities.
